newsitem.title: NORWAY: Scientists use drug to control winter depression.
newsitem.headline: Scientists use drug to control winter depression.

text.p: Scientists said on Sunday they had found a new way to combat a debilitating depression caused by light depravation during winter.

Announcing the results of a trial of an anti-depressant at the end of a two-day conference in the Arctic city of Tromsoe, they said the drug, sertraline, offered new hope for millions of sufferers of seasonal affective disorder (SAD).
"The results of an international clinical trial show there is significant benefit to be gained using sertraline for the treatment of patients with SAD," said a statement from the conference panel.
"These result give patients and scientists alike a reason to be optimistic..."

Sertraline, manufactured by U.S. drug company Pfizer Inc, is widely used in a range of disorders including depression, obsessive-compulsive and panic disorders. It was launched in Britain in 1990 and in the United States in 1992.

SAD, also dubbed "winter depression", is characterised by seasonal depressions. They can start in autumn and are accompanied by symptoms of lethargy, a loss of libido, cravings for carbohydrates, weight gain, anxiety and mood swings.
The condition often vanishes in the spring.

It is especially prevalent in the northern hemisphere where winters tend to be long and dark, but has been recorded in South Africa and Australia. Studies indicate that up to nine percent of the world's population may be afflicted by some form of SAD.
Until now the only proven treatment was light therapy, which requires a patient to sit in front of a light box emitting 10 to 20 times the light of a normal light bulb for up to two hours each day.

Scientists at the Tromsoe conference said they now believed the condition is linked to low levels of serotonin, a chemical messenger known as a neurotransmitter, in the brain. Serotonin is released from neurons when impulses travel between tbe brain's nerve cells.
Sertraline may increase levels of serotonin by blocking its reabsorption into neurons once the impulse has passed through, they say.
Dr Carl Blashko, leader of the trial and associate professor at the University of Alberta in Canada, said patients given the drug showed significant improvement compared with a placebo group.

Carried out at five centres in Austria, Canada, Finland, France and Britain, the trial found that 50 percent of the 93 patients treated with sertraline reported a reduction in depression compared with 30 percent in a placebo group of 94.
Anxiety fell on average by 40 percent with sertraline against 20 percent for placebo.

"We have been searching for years for an effective medication for the treatment of SAD. Now for the first time we have one that has scientific backing of a properly controlled clinical trial," Blashko said.
Jennifer Eastwood, a sufferer of SAD and chairman of the British SAD Association, was a member of the trial group and uses sertraline and light therapy to control the winter blues.
"Light deals with the physical symptoms of SAD, whereas the drug deals better with the core mental symptom, depression. I wouldn't want to carry on living without it," Eastwood said.
